answer_text:
Let

\[
A_n=\sum_{k=1}^n k^a,\qquad 
B_n=(n+1)^{a-1}\sum_{k=1}^n (na+k).
\]

First compute the sum in the denominator:

\[
\sum_{k=1}^n (na+k)=n(na)+\frac{n(n+1)}2
=n^2a+\frac{n(n+1)}2.
\]

Thus

\[
B_n=(n+1)^{a-1}\left(n^2a+\frac{n(n+1)}2\right).
\]

Factor out powers of \(n\):

\[
B_n
=n^{a+1}\left(1+\frac1n\right)^{a-1}
\left(a+\frac12+\frac{1}{2n}\right).
\]

For the numerator, for \(a>-1\), the standard power-sum asymptotic gives

\[
A_n=\sum_{k=1}^n k^a \sim \frac{n^{a+1}}{a+1}.
\]

Therefore, when \(a>-1\) and \(a\neq -\frac12\),

\[
\frac{A_n}{B_n}
\to
\frac{\frac1{a+1}}{a+\frac12}
=
\frac{1}{(a+1)(a+\frac12)}.
\]

We are told this limit equals \(\frac1{60}\), so

\[
\frac{1}{(a+1)(a+\frac12)}=\frac1{60}.
\]

Hence

\[
(a+1)\left(a+\frac12\right)=60.
\]

Expanding,

\[
a^2+\frac32a+\frac12=60,
\]

\[
2a^2+3a-119=0.
\]

Solving,

\[
a=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{9+952}}4
=\frac{-3\pm31}{4}.
\]

So

\[
a=7 \quad \text{or} \quad a=-\frac{17}{2}.
\]

Since the asymptotic formula used requires \(a>-1\), the value \(a=-\frac{17}{2}\) is not admissible. Also, the desired limit is positive finite, which forces \(a>-\frac12\) anyway.

Thus the only valid value is

\[
\boxed{7}.
\]
